newsitem.title: USA: Auto industry continues to boost Tennessee - S&P.
newsitem.headline: Auto industry continues to boost Tennessee - S&P.

text.p: Tennessee's rapid auto industry expansion has acted as a catalyst for job, income and economic growth that is expected to continue, Standard & Poor's Corp said in a report released Monday.

The state's auto presence has continually expanded since Nissan Motor Manufacturing Corp, a unit of Nissan Motor Co Ltd, opened its plant in 1982 in Smyrna, Tenn., and the Saturn Corp followed seven years later with a plant in Spring Hill, Tenn.

"Even more remarkable are the projections for continued auto and related manufacturing expansions and the vital role these sectors will play in stabilizing the state's and some local economies for years to come," S&P said.
The industry is a key factor in the state's AA-plus general obligation bond rating as well as the strength of several credits in the Nashville metro area, S&P said.

Auto manufacturing has contributed to strong direct and indirect job growth in manufacturing spillover jobs and in the service and retail sectors, with three to four jobs created for every one auto job.
Statewide job growth averaged 4.8 percent a year since 1994, while income growth has averaged 4.3 percent, both well ahead of the national average.

Growth in auto and related jobs has led to increased personal income, which in turn has increased demand for housing and services. Sales tax revenue from household goods and the varied retail sector increased throughout the decade. The state relies on sales taxes for 60 percent of its total revenues.

The auto companies have been attracted by the region's lower transporation, labor and living costs and by its access to the majority of the car-buying market. Generous state and local incentive packages, and government willingness to assist with work training have also palyed a role.

The industry's relative insulation from business cycles is linked to the development of a self-contained industry within the state. Unlike other North American car-making centers, Tennessee's auto industry is not a cluster of factories. Both Nissan and Saturn are strategic central production centers.
Local suppliers enable them to compete with the rest of the auto market, and enjoy long-term contracts that reduce the suppliers' vulnerability to changes in models.
Seven major automotive supply companies have recently announced projects in the state for a combined investment of $211 million.

Also contributing to Nissan's success is the fact there are no other Nissan plants in the United States or Canada. Nissan employes more than 7,000 workers in Smyrna, which produces three popular car and pickup truck models.

Constructon is under way on a $30 million engine plant to build the four-cylinder engine and add a $50 million transaxle factory in Decherd, Tenn. Nissan expects total expansion to increase to about $500 million in the coming years, S&P said.
The impact on local credit ratings of strong auto and related employment and income growth is demonstrated by the GO ratings of Rutherford and Maury counties in the Nashville metropolitan area.

Rutherford was upgraded into the AA category after expansions by Nissan and its economic climate is one of steady diversification. Ongoing expansion of the highway system will be important in its continued diversification, S&P said.

Related manufacturers such as tire-maker Bridgestone Corp's Bridgestone USA unit contribute to the auto presence. A spillover of trade and service industry companies formerly located in Nashville, and several warehouse and distribution centers, have added to Rutherford's economic diversity.

Increased per capita income, coupled with affordable single-family housing and proximity to Nashville have more than doubled its tax base since 1988. The county enjoys strong financial operations and reserves, due in large parts to the auto industry growth and its ripple effects.

Saturn has expanded employment by 20 percent since 1993, to 9,000 workers. A subsidiary of General Motors Corp., Saturn produces several popular sedans. Saturn's original 100,000-square foot plant has been expanded by 600,000 square feet in two stages and construction on a 300,000- to 400,000-square-foot extension is expected shortly, S&P said.

Saturn staffed initial operations with relocated GM employees but has increasingly hired local residents. This fulfills a commitment made to the state and supports projections for continued income growth through the millenium, S&P said.

The economy of Maury County, just south of Nashville, is also anchored by Saturn and its expanding workforce. The auto industry has helped boost its population by more than 20 percent since 1994 and contributed to steady growth in its tax base, S&P said.

Maury has less economic diversity than Rutherford County, a factor in its comparitively lower AA-minus bond rating. Unemployment continues to decline and its financial position is strong, in no small part due good financial management.

The county and Saturn entered into a 40-year agreement in which the firm makes payments in lieu of taxes of $3 million for the first 10 years and pays only a percentage of its estimated property value. Payments have increased as Saturn expanded, S&P said.
